text: For a smallholder farmer in Preah Vihear, disease recognition should focus on noticing changes from an animal's normal condition and treating symptoms as warning signs, not a diagnosis. Important cattle diseases to recognize include foot-and-mouth disease (FMD — fever, excessive salivation, mouth/foot lesions, lameness; highly contagious, separate affected animals and seek help promptly), lumpy skin disease (LSD — fever, firm skin nodules, enlarged lymph nodes, reduced production; insects can contribute to transmission), respiratory disease (coughing, nasal discharge, fever, depression, rapid/difficult breathing — many possible causes), and reproductive disease/brucellosis (repeated abortion, stillbirth, infertility, retained placenta — requires veterinary investigation, and farmers should avoid handling potentially contaminated birth materials). Contagious bovine pleuropneumonia (CBPP) is internationally important but its local Cambodian relevance should be confirmed against current animal-health information rather than assumed. During the wet season (roughly May–October), watch animals in muddy/crowded conditions and increased insect activity; during the dry season (roughly November–April), heat stress, reduced forage, and animal movement around water sources complicate monitoring. Practical smallholder response: notice abnormal animals early, separate obviously sick animals where feasible, avoid unnecessary movement/mixing, and contact a veterinarian or animal-health authority promptly for serious or contagious-looking disease. The chatbot should never diagnose FMD, LSD, brucellosis, or CBPP from symptoms alone, and should not provide treatment or medication dosages as though universally appropriate. No specific "common breed" is assigned to Preah Vihear cattle due to insufficient province-specific evidence.
